chunks: "Heat density is the power dissipated per unit area, and it is what sets how hot a part gets.

With a single phase at 60 amps, everything is concentrated in one pair of FETs and one inductor, and on the same parts that one stage would lose almost 9 watts in my example, because conduction loss goes as current squared.
With four phases the total is about 5 watts, divided into four sources of about 1. 3 watts each, spread over four packages and four inductors.
Temperature rise is power times thermal resistance, so each package runs several times cooler than one package carrying everything would.
That spread also gives the board more copper and surface area to take the heat away, and you can place the phases around the load or in a row with airflow.
It isn't a clean one over N.
Per package the loss actually falls faster than that, since conduction drops as one over N squared, but the phases are close together, so they warm each other, and the inner ones run hotter.
And at light load the total can go up, because gate drive and core loss grow with the number of phases.

Either way the peak temperature and the heat density come down, and there is a second benefit, because FET on-resistance and copper resistance rise with temperature, so running cooler also reduces conduction loss a bit.
So at full load multiphase makes somewhat less heat, but the bigger win is that it makes the heat manageable."
